beats.caption: Two networks: scale-up inside the rack, scale-out between racks
beats.text: An AI cluster has two separate fabrics. Scale-up ties a group of accelerators (here 72 GPUs in one rack) together with very fast, memory-like links so they behave as one machine. Scale-out connects thousands of those groups across the building with Ethernet or InfiniBand. Each GPU is wired to both.

beats.caption: Scale-up: copper links, memory-speed, a few metres
beats.text: Inside the rack every GPU links through NVSwitch trays over a copper cable spine (NVLink, or UALink in open designs). GPUs load and store directly into each other's memory with sub-microsecond latency. Copper keeps it cheap and low-power, but it only reaches a couple of metres, which caps the domain at roughly a rack.

beats.caption: Scale-out: NICs, optics and switch tiers across the hall
beats.text: To leave the rack, data goes through a NIC (one per GPU), an optical transceiver and fibre to a leaf switch, up to a spine and back down. It is packet networking with RDMA, so it reaches any of 100,000 GPUs, at the cost of more hops, more latency and less bandwidth per GPU.

beats.caption: Each GPU gets about 18x more bandwidth on scale-up
beats.text: A Blackwell GPU has 1.8 TB/s of NVLink but one 800 Gb/s NIC, about 100 GB/s, for scale-out. So model work is split to match: tensor and expert parallelism (chatty, every layer) stays inside the scale-up domain, data and pipeline parallelism (larger, rarer transfers) cross the scale-out network.

beats.caption: Two markets: a contested new one and a big established one
beats.text: Scale-up is newer and fought over: Nvidia's proprietary NVLink against open UALink and Ethernet-based scale-up, with retimers and copper cables in between. Scale-out is the existing Ethernet/InfiniBand switch, NIC and optics market, and companies report the two separately. Related: NVDA, AVGO, ALAB, ANET, MRVL.
